description: What AppleFontSmoothing 0 to 3 does on macOS 27.2 (1, 2 and 3 draw identical pixels), subpixel versus greyscale antialiasing, ClearType and hinting, why external monitors look worse on a Mac, what 0 costs or saves, and how it differs from turning antialiasing off. Four live demos.
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. Every demo above redraws live.
disclosure: Measured on macOS 27.2. The value sweep, the stem widths and the CSS checks come from AppKit, WebKit and Chrome renders on an Apple silicon Mac whose system setting is 0. The demos redraw text with this page's own rasterizer and a growth model fitted to those renders, so they show the mechanism the same way in every browser. As a control, the model's ink for 13 pt Helvetica lands within 3 percentage points of AppKit's in all four cases (1x and 2x, both polarities). The history and the Windows side are paraphrased from the linked sources.

editorial.reader: A Mac user on an external monitor who pasted the AppleFontSmoothing command from a forum and wants to know what it changes.
editorial.problem: The reader can see that text on their monitor looks worse than on a MacBook or on Windows, and can't say which step of text rendering causes it or what the values 0 to 3 change.
editorial.thesis: On macOS 27.2 AppleFontSmoothing is a switch that thickens stems by up to 0.6 px, and external monitors look worse because macOS dropped subpixel rendering, never snaps stems to the pixel grid, and tunes everything for 2x.
evidence: A 48-case AppKit sweep renders byte-identical bitmaps for 1, 2 and 3, and only 0 differs.
Stem measurements from 9 to 96 pt fit growth of 0.0116 px per ppem for dark text and 0.032 for light text, capped at 0.6 px.
With the system at 0, Chrome and WebKit draw the same pixels for every -webkit-font-smoothing value.
Timed AppKit draws show smoothing adds about 20% to first rasterization and nothing once glyphs are cached, and antialiasing off draws 2 grey levels against 224 at 0.
editorial.uncertainty: I measured one Mac on one OS release with the system set to 0, so the browser path with smoothing left on rests on MDN, and the Windows side rests on the cited sources.

understanding.intro: Before you close the window: 7 questions, no grades. Every demo above still runs if you want to check an answer against it.

questions.q: You set AppleFontSmoothing to 3 and relaunch an app on macOS 27.2. Compared with 1, what changes on screen?

options.t: nothing at all, since 1 and 3 grow every stem by exactly the same amount
options.why: The 48-case sweep produced byte-identical bitmaps for 1, 2 and 3. The light, medium and strong names belong to the LCD era.

options.t: stems thicken about three times as much, since the value scales the growth
options.why: That's a fair reading of the Snow Leopard names. On 27.2 the value only switches the growth on, and its size comes from pixels per em.

options.t: text switches to subpixel rendering, since 3 was the strong LCD setting
options.why: Subpixel rendering left with Mojave. No value of this key brings the colored stripes back.

questions.q: In the dial demo, leave the dial at 2, set size to 24 pt and screen to 2x, Retina. Now flip text from black on white to white on black. What does the 'every stem grows by' readout do?

options.t: it creeps from 0.56 px to 0.60 px, since both now sit at or near the cap
options.why: A 2x screen doubles pixels per em, so 24 pt is 48 ppem. Black text grows 0.0116 x 48 = 0.56 px, and white text's 0.032 x 48 = 1.54 px gets cut to the 0.6 px cap. So the 2.75x asymmetry is a low-ppem story: it shows in full at 13 pt on a 1x screen, where the page measures 0.15 px against 0.41.

options.t: it jumps from 0.56 px to 1.54 px, since light text grows 2.75 times faster
options.why: The rate is right and the cap is missing. Growth stops at 0.6 px. On a 2x screen black text reaches that near 26 pt, and white text, growing 2.75 times faster, gets there far sooner. Which number in the chat's growth rule did 1.54 skip?

options.t: it jumps from 0.28 px to 0.77 px, since growth scales with the point size
options.why: Growth follows pixels per em, and the screen setting doubles them: 24 pt on 2x is 48 ppem. The readout itself says 'at 48 pixels per em'. Even on points, 0.77 px would overshoot the 0.6 px cap.

options.t: it stays at 0.56 px, since polarity only changes how heavy text looks
options.why: Polarity changes the outline itself. The page's 13 pt measurement on 1x had dark-mode stems gaining 0.41 px against 0.15 for black text. Here the gap shrinks because white text hits the cap, and the readout still moves.

questions.q: Subpixel rendering gives sharper edges on a 1x LCD. What made it a poor fit for a GPU-composited desktop?

options.t: it needs the background color at raster time, since each stripe blends alone
options.why: One alpha can blend over anything later. Three alphas need the color behind the glyph before compositing has decided it.

options.t: it needs a Retina display, since stripes are too small to address at 1x
options.why: Backwards. Subpixel rendering pays off most at 1x, where a third of a pixel is still large enough to matter.

options.t: it triples the size of every font file, since each glyph ships three outlines
options.why: A font ships one outline per glyph. The cost lands in the glyph cache at render time, which grows with every subpixel offset.

questions.q: In the monitor demo, pick the 27-inch 5K and switch its mode from 'looks like 2560x1440' to 'looks like 3200x1800'. What does the table report?

options.t: it draws at 6400x3600, then resamples by 0.800, just like a 4K at 2560
options.why: macOS draws every HiDPI mode at twice its looks-like size, so 3200 becomes 6400, and 5120 / 6400 = 0.8. Exact 2x belongs to the mode: the same panel at 2560x1440 resamples by nothing. So on a 5K, asking for more space buys back the double filtering 4K owners live with.

options.t: nothing gets resampled, since 5K is the exact-2x panel macOS is built for
options.why: Exact fit is a property of the mode, and the demo shows it: the 5K's 2560x1440 default reads 'nothing, exact fit', and 3200x1800 doesn't. Nothing is resampled only when twice the looks-like width equals the panel's 5120.

options.t: macOS sends 3200x1800 and the monitor's own scaler stretches it to 5K
options.why: The table's second row says macOS draws at 6400x3600. Every HiDPI mode runs the same way on the Mac: draw at twice the looks-like size, then resample to the panel's native pixels.

options.t: it draws at 6400x3600, then resamples by 1.250 to reach the panel
options.why: The frame size is right and the direction isn't. A 6400-wide frame has to shrink to fit 5120 pixels, so the factor is 5120 / 6400 = 0.800. 1.25 is how much more room you asked for, which is exactly why the frame comes out too big.

questions.q: A forum reply says: 'AppleFontSmoothing 0 turns antialiasing off, which is why text gets crisper, like Windows.' What's wrong with it?

options.t: 0 keeps antialiasing and drops only the stem growth, so edges stay grey
options.why: The page counted grey levels on one 13 pt line: 224 at 0, 229 with smoothing on, and 2 with antialiasing actually off. 0 drops the thickening and keeps the greys. The 'like Windows' half fails too, since Windows gets its crisp columns from hinting, which no value of this key turns on.

options.t: nothing: 0 is the off position, and the old checkbox called it smoothing
options.why: The checkbox and the key both named the thickening. The measurement settles it: 224 grey levels at 0, against 2 with antialiasing switched off in the graphics context. Pick 1-bit in the letter demo to see what off looks like: stairs.

options.t: only the Windows part: its text is crisper because of ClearType alone
options.why: That clause is shaky, and ClearType is only half of it: hinting snaps the stem to whole columns before the stripes go on, which the stem demo's bottom two rows show. The bigger error is up front. 0 leaves 224 grey levels on a 13 pt line.

options.t: 0 turns it off, but only below the AppleAntiAliasingThreshold size
options.why: That threshold is a separate key, and on 27.2 it changed nothing measurable: set to 14, it left 13 pt text antialiased. AppleFontSmoothing drops the growth at every size and leaves antialiasing alone.

questions.q: Where does the extra cost of smoothing land when you scroll a long page?

options.t: almost nowhere, since each glyph is thickened once and then cached
options.why: Fresh rasterization ran about 20% slower with smoothing on, and drawing cached glyphs took 41 to 44 ms either way.

options.t: on every frame, since the GPU thickens each glyph again as it composites
options.why: The growth happens on the CPU when the glyph is rasterized. The compositor only moves the finished bitmap.

options.t: on every line, since each new line of text is rasterized again from outlines
options.why: A new line reuses glyphs already in the cache. Only a letter at a size the cache hasn't seen gets rasterized.

questions.q: Your 27-inch 1440p monitor runs dark mode, and you set AppleFontSmoothing 0 hoping 13 pt text will look like Windows on the same panel. What do you get?

options.t: lighter, even stems that stay soft, since stripes and hinting don't return
options.why: At 109 PPI macOS draws at 1x, and dark mode is where growth bites hardest: 0 strips the 0.41 px that made the stem 36% heavier. The 1.14 px stem still straddles two columns as two greys, since 0 restores neither subpixel stripes nor hinting. That's why the page says no setting makes 109 PPI on a Mac look like ClearType.

options.t: Windows-sharp text, since 0 hands the stems back to grid snapping
options.why: Snapping is hinting, and macOS skips it at every value of the key. Drag the stem demo: the two macOS rows always spread a 1.14 px stem over two or more columns, and only the snapped to the grid row holds it to one dark column.

options.t: no visible change, since smoothing only thickens text on Retina screens
options.why: Growth tracks pixels per em on any screen. At 1x it adds 0.41 px to a 1.14 px dark-mode stem, and the monitor demo's verdict for a 1x panel under 150 PPI is that this is where AppleFontSmoothing 0 earns its keep.

options.t: lighter stems, but only by the 0.15 px that black-on-white text gains
options.why: Lighter, yes, and by more: 0.15 px is the black-on-white growth at 13 pt. White on black grows 2.75 times faster, so dark mode sheds 0.41 px, the biggest saving the key offers on this panel.

messages.html: first thing i run on any new mac: defaults -currentHost write -g AppleFontSmoothing -int 0. what is that actually changing, and what do 1, 2 and 3 do?

It writes one integer into this Mac's global preferences. -g is the domain every app reads, and -currentHost files the value under this machine's hardware UUID in ~/Library/Preferences/ByHost/, where the old System Preferences checkbox kept it. AppKit reads the key when an app launches, so an app that's already open keeps its old text until you quit it.

The numbers date from Snow Leopard. That release cut the Appearance pane down to one checkbox, and a Terminal command became the only way back to the old menu: 1 for light, 2 for medium and 3 for strong LCD smoothing.

cite.title: Macworld, 2009: Enable better font smoothing on some LCD displays in Snow Leopard

messages.html: So I swept them on macOS 27.2: Helvetica, the system font, Tahoma and Verdana, at 11, 13 and 16 pt, at 1x and 2x, as black-on-white and as white-on-black. In all 48 cases, 1, 2 and 3 drew byte-identical bitmaps, and only 0 differed. The key is a switch now. Any value above 0 means on.

demo.html:
This draws the text itself, with the growth model fitted to those renders, so it shows the macOS mechanism in any browser, Windows included. The row follows the dial. The magnifier beside it shows one square per pixel as the 0 render, turning orange where smoothing adds ink.

messages.html: ok so what is "on" doing to the letters?

It fattens them. AppKit grows every outline a little before it fills it, so each stem widens on both edges. I measured the stem of a Helvetica l: at 13 pt on a 1x screen it's 1.14 px wide at 0 and 1.30 px with smoothing on.

The growth tracks pixels per em, about 0.0116 px per ppem, and stops at 0.6 px, which a 2x screen reaches near 26 pt. White text on black grows 2.75 times faster, 0.032 px per ppem, so the same 13 pt stem in dark mode lands at 1.55 px, 36% heavier than at 0. That asymmetry is why light-on-dark text gains the most when you set 0.
and subpixel vs greyscale antialiasing? i've seen both blamed for this

Both answer one question per pixel: how much of it does the letter cover? Greyscale antialiasing turns that fraction into a shade, so a pixel half inside a stem becomes 50% grey. All three color channels get the same value, which lets the text sit on any background, under any blend or animation.

Subpixel rendering notices that an LCD pixel is three vertical stripes, red, green and blue, and asks the question three times per pixel. Edges can land on a third of a pixel, which triples horizontal resolution. The price is color: an edge that covers only the red stripe tints red, so a filter spreads each third into its neighbours until the fringe fades.

demo.bar: one letter, magnified · switch the fill
demo.html: A 13 px Georgia letter, drawn three ways and blown up so each square is one pixel. Shift it sideways by part of a pixel and watch the edge shading move. Tick stripes to see what the panel actually lights.

messages.html: subpixel sounds strictly better. why would apple remove it?

Mojave turned it off in 2018, and the reason lives in the compositor. Greyscale coverage is one alpha value, so the GPU can blend a finished glyph onto anything. Subpixel coverage is three alphas, one per stripe, so the renderer has to know the exact color behind the glyph at the moment it rasterizes. A translucent, layer-backed, animated desktop hasn't decided that color yet.

An ex-macOS engineer listed the rest on Hacker News during the Mojave beta: the panel's stripe geometry threaded through every graphics layer, glyph caches multiplied by every subpixel offset, and artifacts whenever text switched between static and animated. Rotate the panel, or use an OLED without RGB stripes, and the three-stripe assumption breaks outright.

What survived is the thickening. Mojave's checkbox became "Use font smoothing when available" and drove only that, and Big Sur deleted the checkbox, which left the defaults key as the only switch.

cite.title: Hacker News, 2018: macOS Mojave removes subpixel anti-aliasing

messages.html: how does windows handle the same problem?

It made the opposite bet, twice. ClearType is subpixel rendering, and Windows Vista made it the system default. Windows fonts also lean on hinting: small programs inside the font that move outlines onto the pixel grid before rasterizing, so a stem that would cover 1.14 px snaps to one whole, dark column.

Joel Spolsky drew the split in 2007. Apple keeps each typeface's true shape and accepts some blur; Microsoft hammers letters onto pixel boundaries and accepts some distortion. Newer Windows frameworks soften both bets, since DirectWrite can place glyphs at fractions of a pixel and modern Windows UI text renders in greyscale.

This site's chrome copies Windows XP, which shipped with ClearType off: its default was greyscale smoothing, the same as Windows 2000, because plenty of desks still had CRTs.

cite.title: Joel Spolsky, 2007: Font smoothing, anti-aliasing, and sub-pixel rendering

demo.bar: one stem, six pixels · drag it across the grid
demo.html: One vertical stem, as wide as a 13 pt Helvetica l on a 1x screen. The top two rows render it the macOS way, greyscale and unhinted; the second adds the 0.15 px that smoothing grows at that size. The bottom two snap it to the grid first, the way hinted fonts on Windows do, and the last adds ClearType's stripes and filter.

messages.html: which gets to my actual complaint. why does a mac look so much worse than windows on the same external monitor?

Because macOS prices every one of those choices for about 220 PPI, and the common 24- and 27-inch monitors sit between 92 and 109. A 27-inch 1440p panel is 109 PPI, so macOS draws it at 1x. There the 13 pt stem is 1.14 px wide, and with no hinting it straddles two columns as two greys. No stripes sharpen its edges. Then smoothing adds 0.15 px of grey on top, or 0.42 px in dark mode. Windows on the same panel snaps the stem to one column and resolves its edges in thirds.

A 27-inch 4K panel has a different problem. Its exact 2x mode looks like 1920x1080, which most owners find too large, so they pick "looks like 2560x1440". macOS draws that at 5120x2880 and then shrinks the whole frame by 0.75 to fit 3840 pixels, so every glyph gets filtered a second time after it was drawn. The external panels that look like a MacBook Pro are the ones where 2x lands exactly on native: 5K at 27 inches and 6K at 32. The MacBook Air's own default mode resamples by 0.871, so even Apple ships the second filter, on pixels half the size of a 1440p panel's.

demo.bar: pick a monitor · see what macOS does to it
demo.html: Pick a panel and a display mode. The numbers come from the panel's geometry and from how macOS runs a HiDPI mode: it draws at twice the "looks like" size, then resamples to the panel's native pixels.

messages.html:
On a 1x monitor I think so. It strips 13% of extra width from black-on-white stems and 36% from white-on-black, and the text stays soft but gets lighter and more even. It can't restore subpixel rendering or hinting, so no setting makes 109 PPI on a Mac look like ClearType. On a Retina screen it comes down to taste: 0.3 px on a 2.3 px stem reads as weight, and the stems are wide enough that their grey edges barely show.

Web pages get the same switch per element. In Safari and Chrome on a Mac, -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased asks for the 0 rendering. The other direction is closed. With the system at 0, I measured subpixel-antialiased drawing the same pixels as antialiased in both Chrome and WebKit, so CSS can switch the thickening off and has no way to switch it back on.
does turning it off help performance at all?

Barely, and only once per glyph. The thickening happens when a glyph is rasterized, before it lands in the glyph cache. I timed AppKit drawing a 33-character Helvetica line 3,000 times, each run seven times. At 3,000 different sizes, so every glyph rasterized fresh, 0 took 380 to 397 ms and smoothing on took 464 to 473 ms, about 20% more. Two separate runs at 0 differed by only 17 ms, so the gap is real.

Drawing the same 13 pt line 3,000 times took 41 to 44 ms either way, because every glyph after the first came from the cache. That's the everyday case: a page of text reuses the same letters at the same few sizes, so smoothing costs about a microsecond per glyph the first time and nothing after. Set 0 for how text looks. Nothing will feel faster.
and is 0 the same as turning antialiasing off?

No. 0 keeps antialiasing and drops only the thickening. I drew one 13 pt Helvetica line three ways and counted its distinct grey levels: 224 at smoothing 0, 229 with smoothing on, and 2 with antialiasing switched off in the graphics context, which leaves pure black and white. With antialiasing off the smoothing value stops mattering, since 0 and 1 drew identical 1-bit pixels.

The old Appearance pane did have a real antialiasing switch, "Turn off text smoothing for font sizes N and smaller", stored as AppleAntiAliasingThreshold. On 27.2 it changed nothing I could measure: set to 14, it left 13 pt text antialiased in an offscreen render. The letter demo above shows what that switch used to do. Pick 1-bit and the curves turn into stairs.
